topic: Requirement-Ledger: From Vibe Coding to Requirements
summary: A 'requirement ledger' is the counter-move to vibe coding: instead of writing a spec before you start, you mine the AI-agent conversation you already had and reconstruct what the user actually required. The anchor artifact is adand-91/requirement-ledger (MIT, Python 3.10-3.13, zero runtime deps), which has since been RENAMED at the repo level to adand-91/gpt-6-astra-skill and repositioned as 'Astra Skill Optimizer' (124 stars, 8 forks, 4 watchers, 0 open issues, 38 commits by a single author, 7 releases from v0.1.0 2026-08-28 to v1.0.0 2026-09-09, last push 2026-09-16). It is NOT on PyPI — install is git-clone-as-skill, not pip install. Its pipeline is: explicit Codex/Claude/text transcript + test log + read-only Git snapshot -> private evidence -> conservative attribution (upstream / project-local / personal / unknown) -> quote-free report + DRAFT (never sent, never applied) repair plan -> host-owned Codex patch -> digest-bound oracle before/after result. v0.1 explicitly does not autonomously edit the project. The academic mirror is AfterVibe (arXiv 2607.09900), which recovers a natural-language spec from a vibe-coding trajectory and validates it with a regeneration test (a blind agent rebuilds the artifact from the spec alone); on 72 real-world vibe-coded tasks the recovered specs scored a mean 5.06/6.0 across multiple independent regenerations (5.74/6.0 after iterative strengthening). The engineering mirror is Justin Chase's Real Polite Protocol authority chain: RFC/spec > requirement documents > requirement tests > scenarios > implementation, with mirrored file paths and an absolute rule that a failing test is never weakened. The why-now case is quantitative: agents now write ~47% of code (JetBrains, 15,509 devs), 74% of orgs say at least a quarter of AI code needs significant rework, and median PR review time is up 441.5%. The gap is not generation — it is that the intent behind the change evaporates when the chat closes.

competitors.title: adand-91/requirement-ledger (repo now resolves to adand-91/gpt-6-astra-skill) — the anchor tool
key_points: Positioning: 'A local, privacy-first evidence loop for improving any Git project with Codex or another coding agent.' Tagline: 'From vibe coding to knowing what you actually wanted.'
Explicitly not autonomous: v0.1 gathers and structures evidence; Codex remains the developer; every real modification stays visible and reviewable.

Pipeline: explicit Codex/Claude/text input + test log + read-only Git snapshot -> private evidence -> conservative attribution -> quote-free report + DRAFT repair plan -> host-owned Codex patch -> digest-bound oracle before/after result.
Versioned record types: SourceRef, EvidenceItem, IssueRecord, FixProposal, ValidationResult.
Four attribution fields — upstream, project-local, personal, unknown — with 'unknown' as the honest default.
Privacy mechanics: physically separate private evidence from quote-free reports, restrictive file modes, non-overwrite writes, fail-closed privacy gate, no remote URLs ever read or emitted.
No hidden patch/commit/push/issue/PR/release/upload/telemetry. Repair plans are stamped 'DRAFT — NOT SENT, not-applied'.
One rule for numbers: every number comes from the script; the model never estimates one. Counting messages by eye is described as 'the failure this skill exists to prevent'.
Real session scale constraint: sessions reach 250 MB with single lines up to 1.5 M chars of base64, so transcripts are streamed line by line, never loaded whole (~1 GB per 3 seconds).
Repo-level rename happened: package/CLI keep 'requirement-ledger' as a compatibility entry point while the public product identity became 'Astra Skill Optimizer'.

competitors.title: AfterVibe: What Remains When the Conversation Ends (arXiv 2607.09900, cs.SE)
key_points: Reframes the problem: vibe coding undermines the assumption that someone can read and vouch for the code; intent lives ephemerally in a chat transcript and the mapping between intent and code is 'implicit at best'.
Treats requirements as implicit — whatever is observable from the session (prompts, corrections, accepted behaviours) is treated as a sufficient expression of requirements.

Core validation idea: a regeneration test — a second, blind AI agent rebuilds the artifact from the spec alone, then a three-tier verifier (flexible test execution, verification conditions extracted from the trajectory, ground-truth alignment via structured LLM reasoning) judges equivalence.
Spec quality is operationalised as 'can an agent regenerate passing code from it', not as human review.
Desiderata in tension: strong (a satisfactory implementation follows from the spec) vs abstract (captures behavioural intent without prescribing implementation).

Environmental grounding hypothesis: a spec only needs to be concrete for undiscoverable facts — decisions, thresholds, domain constraints — because the agent can navigate the repo for build config, naming, module structure, API contracts.

Evaluation: 72 real-world vibe-coded tasks from an industrial monorepo; mean regeneration score 5.06/6.0 across multiple independent regenerations (5.74/6.0 after iterative strengthening), with regenerations staying diverse in their details.
Claims to be the first to pursue requirements traceability directly from human-AI coding trajectories.

competitors.title: Justin Chase — the authority chain on Real Polite Protocol (field report)
key_points: The diagnostic: 'the tests pass' is a much weaker signal than it used to be because the agent wrote the code and the tests, both optimizing to satisfy a prompt typed two minutes ago.

The reviewer's squeeze: agents produce more code per unit time than any reviewer can meaningfully read, and the prompts justifying the code are ephemeral — by the time drift is visible the conversation is gone.

A strict written authority order every change must respect: RFC / spec -> requirement documents -> requirement tests -> scenarios -> implementation code; a lower-authority artifact must not contradict a higher-authority one.
When a test fails the implementation is fixed; the test is never weakened. Changing behaviour means changing the requirement deliberately and explicitly first.
Requirement documents are the smallest reviewable unit of intent; if the code diff is large and the requirement diff is empty, something is wrong.

Requirement tests mirror requirement paths exactly, which makes structural coverage analysis trivial — a script can report a requirement with no test, or a test with no requirement, without reading either.

Durable context effect: the requirement files accumulate a structured record of every behaviour the system has committed to, so an agent reasons against decided behaviour rather than against today's code.
Answers the 'this is waterfall in a trench coat' objection: the spec governs what the system does, not how; the how lives in a separate, orthogonal instructions layer.

competitors.title: Birgitta Böckeler (Thoughtworks, on martinfowler.com) — the SDD taxonomy to position against
key_points: Definition still in flux: SDD means writing a 'spec' before writing code with AI (documentation first), with the spec as source of truth for human and AI.

Three maturity levels: spec-first (spec written first, used for the task at hand), spec-anchored (spec kept after the task to drive evolution and maintenance), spec-as-source (spec is the main source file; the human only ever edits the spec).
Key nuance: all SDD approaches are spec-first, but not all strive to be spec-anchored or spec-as-source — and tools often leave that vague.
Vendor framing quoted: GitHub — 'maintaining software means evolving specifications… code is the last-mile approach'; Tessl — 'specs, not code, are the primary artifact'.
Directly relevant to the ledger: the taxonomy is about specs before code; the requirement ledger is retrospective — it recovers the spec after the conversation, which is a different axis entirely.

competitors.title: François Zaninotto (Marmelab) — the strongest published objection
key_points: SDD 'revives the old idea of heavy documentation before coding — an echo of the Waterfall era' and risks burying agility under layers of Markdown.
Names the toolkit landscape: Spec-Kit (GitHub), Kiro (AWS), Tessl, BMad Method.
Concrete bloat evidence: a spec-kit run for a single small feature (display the current date in a time-tracking app) produced 8 files and 1,300 lines of text.
Kiro example for a small CRM feature (adding a 'referred by' field) produced Requirements.md + Design.md + Tasks.md.
Argument to answer in the guide: an iterative natural-language approach may fit modern development better than document-first ceremony.

competitors.title: ONES.com — AI requirement management agents for vibe coding collaboration (commercial comparison)
key_points: Buyer framing that validates the keyword: 'the bottleneck moved from writing code to keeping human intent and AI output in sync.'
Failure symptoms named: backlog full of half-finished features, orphaned branches, requirements nobody can trace back to a decision.
The exclusion criterion offered: reject tools that 'bolt an AI assistant onto a generic task tracker without built-in review coordination and requirements-to-delivery traceability.'
Compares ONES, Linear, ClickUp, GitHub Projects, GitLab, Azure DevOps on requirement-to-agent-task breakdown, repository context retention, and delivery governance.
Commercial and platform-level: it is about a governance layer in a PM tool, not a local evidence artifact in your repo — the local-first angle is the differentiator to claim.

competitors.title: Foxfire1st/agents-remember — adjacent 'epistemic ledger' for coding agents
key_points: Self-description: 'A branch-aware, dual-revision epistemic ledger and control plane for AI coding agents. From requirements and isolated work to validated changes and durable, queryable project truth.'
27 stars, 4 forks, MIT, created 2026-03-21, last push 2026-09-28 — so 'ledger for agents' is a live naming trend, not one repo.
Topic tags show the shape: bitemporal, dual-revision, path-addressed memory, worktree-isolation, versioned-memory, MCP server.
Distinguishes itself from the anchor tool by being a control plane with queryable memory rather than a privacy-first retrospection CLI.
Useful as the 'same idea, different architecture' comparison so the article is not a single-tool review.

angles: The reversal nobody planned for: the spec is now recovered after the fact, not written before. Vibe coding's cheap fix is not a better upfront spec document — it is mining the corrections the user already made, because every course correction is a place where the delivered thing and the wanted thing diverged.

Corrections are the requirement. The first message states what the user asked for; the last correction states what they actually needed. A ledger built from the opening prompt is a ledger of the wrong thing.

Retrospective vs prospective is the real axis. SDD (Fowler's spec-first / spec-anchored / spec-as-source) is prospective; a requirement ledger is retrospective. They are complements, and the guide should refuse the framing that the ledger is 'SDD with extra steps'.

Numbers you can defend. The one rule of the anchor tool — every number comes from a script, the model never estimates one — is a transferable discipline: a retrospective with invented counts is worse than none because it gets quoted later as fact.

'Unknown' as the honest default. Four attribution buckets (upstream, project-local, personal, unknown) with unknown defaulted rather than guessed is a governance pattern that generalises well beyond this tool.

Privacy is the unglamorous feature. Transcripts hitting 250 MB with 1.5 M-character base64 lines mean the naive approach (paste the log into the model) fails on both cost and blast radius; streaming, quote-free reports and a fail-closed gate are engineering, not marketing.

The authority chain answers the waterfall objection. Spec governs what, instructions govern how; a failing test is never weakened; the requirement diff is the one a reviewer actually reads. That is the concrete rebuttal to 'this is waterfall in a trench coat'.

Prove the ledger works with a regeneration test. If a blind agent can rebuild the change from your recovered spec and pass the same after-test, the spec is strong; that is a measurable acceptance criterion instead of a feeling.

Read the repo name, not the blog post. The anchor project was renamed mid-flight to 'Astra Skill Optimizer' with a Jarvis long-term roadmap, while the CLI keeps the old name as a compatibility entry point — a live example of intent drift, which is exactly the failure mode the tool exists to catch.

The bottleneck moved. Review time now exceeds writing time (11.4 h vs 9.8 h per week) and median review latency is up 441.5%; 74% of orgs say a quarter or more of AI code needs significant rework. A ledger is a review-capacity tool before it is a documentation tool.

outline: H2: Why vibe-coded projects lose their requirements (intent lives in a chat transcript; 47% of code is agent-written, and when the conversation closes the justification is gone)
H2: What a requirement ledger actually is — and what it is not (local evidence loop, not an autonomous fixer; v0.1 never edits your project)
H2: Corrections are the requirement: reading the conversation backwards (first message vs last correction; course corrections as divergence points)

H2: The evidence chain, step by step (explicit agent transcript + test log + read-only Git snapshot -> private evidence -> conservative attribution -> quote-free report + DRAFT repair plan -> host-owned patch -> digest-bound before/after result)
H2: Four attribution buckets, with 'unknown' as the honest default (upstream, project-local, personal, unknown)
H2: Set up requirement-ledger with Claude Code or Codex (git clone as a skill, Python 3.10-3.13, zero runtime deps, not on PyPI; scan_transcript.py facts-first; 60-second synthetic demo)
H2: Numbers come from the script, never from the model (why an invented count in a retrospective is worse than no count)

H2: Mirrored requirement tests and the authority chain (spec > requirements > requirement tests > scenarios > implementation; a failing test is never weakened; the requirement diff is the one that matters)

H2: How this differs from spec-driven development (spec-first vs spec-anchored vs spec-as-source vs retrospective recovery; why the ledger is not waterfall, and the 1,300-line spec-kit counter-example)
H2: Prove the ledger works: the regeneration test (blind re-implementation from the spec alone, three-tier verification, 5.06/6.0 on 72 tasks)
H2: Privacy and blast radius (250 MB sessions, 1.5 M-char base64 lines, streaming instead of pasting, separate private evidence from quote-free reports, fail-closed gate, no telemetry)
H2: Adoption reality check for 2026 (single-contributor 124-star project, 7 releases, a mid-flight rename to Astra Skill Optimizer, 0 open issues; what is proven vs experimental)
H2: Getting started checklist (write the authority chain down first, add requirement files one PR at a time, pin them to tests, review the requirement diff before the code diff)
